facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: The financial base for American is a highly levered airline whose reported earnings fell in 2026 while its balance sheet was kept intact by refinancing. On the issuer's own statements, operating income for the nine months of 2026 was 535 against 1,042 a year earlier, with fuel expense up by 4,427 over the same nine months, and the third quarter alone produced a pre-tax loss of 183. Last-twelve-month EBITDA, derived here as operating income plus depreciation and amortization, is 2,916, against 3,395 in FY2025 and 4,573 in FY2024. Gross debt including finance leases is 25,876 and net debt after unrestricted cash and short-term investments is 17,623, so net leverage is 6.04x and cash interest cover is 2.06x, both weaker than FY2025. Liquidity is large at 11,763 but was built partly through 5,933 of new debt, and the filings put 7,861 of principal due in 2028 plus a very large set of purchase commitments behind it. Parent-level facts matter for this issuer: American guarantees three parent promissory notes and carries a net 10,430 receivable from related parties, mainly the parent. Confidence in the base is medium, because the metrics are calculated by this analysis from filed statements and several covenant and document inputs are not supplied.

facts.label: Earnings and cash flow quality
facts.text: Evidence: American's revenue for the nine months of 2026 was 46,979 against 40,628, an increase of 6,351, while fuel expense rose from 8,017 to 12,444, an increase of 4,427, and operating income fell from 1,042 to 535. In the third quarter revenue was 16,334 against 13,688, fuel 4,635 against 2,767, and operating income 114 against 167. Mechanism: fuel absorbed about seven tenths of the nine-month revenue gain (4,427 of 6,351, calculated below), and other cost lines (salaries, wages and benefits 14,019 against 13,058) rose as well, so incremental revenue converted to very little operating profit. The filing states that the company does not hedge fuel (Q3 10-Q page:45, "Our current policy is not to enter into transactions to hedge our fuel consumption"), so the exposure is open. Implication: coverage is thin, and a further fuel increase flows straight to EBITDA, which is the denominator of both leverage and interest cover.

facts.text: Operating cash flow of 4,440 for the nine months against 2,229 looks strong but has a specific source: the filing attributes the increase mainly to working capital increases in air traffic liability and loyalty program liability and to changes in net receivables from related parties (Q3 10-Q page:63). facts.label: Leverage and coverage
facts.text: Gross leverage is calculated on balance-sheet debt and finance leases, because that is the only debt aggregate the issuer statements print as a sum of components; net leverage deducts cash and short-term investments (not restricted cash). On this basis total debt over LTM EBITDA is 8.87x at 2026-09-30, against 7.44x at 2025-12-31 and 5.63x at 2024-12-31, and net debt over EBITDA is 6.04x, against 5.73x and 4.10x. Net debt itself fell from 19,443 to 17,623 over the nine months because cash and short-term investments rose from 5,816 to 8,253 while gross debt rose from 25,259 to 25,876; the ratio nevertheless rose because LTM EBITDA fell from 3,395 to 2,916. Mechanism: the cash build was funded by 5,933 of new borrowing in the nine months, so net leverage improves in dollars but not in ratio and the cash carries interest cost. Cash interest cover (EBITDA over interest paid, net) is 2.06x LTM, against 2.19x in FY2025 and 2.53x in FY2024. Interest paid is the issuer's net figure and the filing does not say whether it nets capitalised interest or interest income, which limits the measure.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: American is the main operating airline of AAG, a listed holding company, and it is the issuer whose creditors this review serves. The business is a hub-based network carrier whose revenue is overwhelmingly passenger, with a loyalty program and co-branded card relationships that provide cash and collateral, and whose cost base is dominated by fuel, labor and regional capacity purchased from carriers under the parent. There is no financial sponsor, no pending acquisition and no dividend recapitalisation in the sources; the transaction record for the period is a sequence of refinancings, aircraft financings and facility amendments, plus a small set of aircraft purchase decisions in October 2026 after quarter end. The governance picture is Mixed rather than Supportive or Adverse: the parent guarantees a large share of American's debt and American guarantees parent notes and funds the parent through intercompany balances, both documented actions, while American has also repaid its own secured debt early. The main creditor consequences are structural (support running in both directions, secured debt ranking ahead of unsecured claims and collateral that includes the loyalty business) and operational (open fuel exposure and heavy fleet commitments). Confidence is medium because executed documents, ratings and any information after the Q3 10-Q are not supplied.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: New debt in the period: American issued enhanced equipment trust certificates in several series. In March 2026 it borrowed 870 million of junior financing secured on aircraft already delivered (the 2026-1 Class (B)R financing, fixed rate 5.61 percent, maturing 2028 to 2029). In May 2026 it created the 2026-1 pass-through trusts (about 1.1 billion face, 32 aircraft). In June 2026 it issued 567 million of engine EETCs to refinance 228 million at maturity and raise 339 million of new borrowing. In August 2026 it created the 2026-2 trusts (about 1.3 billion face, 37 aircraft), of which about 692 million had been used to buy equipment notes at 2026-09-30 and about 633 million was held in escrow for holders, not reported as American's debt. It also borrowed 705 million of variable-rate equipment loans on aircraft. The use of proceeds is aircraft financing, and the filing states that proceeds of the nine months totalled about 4.1 billion for EETCs, equipment loans and other notes (page:46).

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Refinancing and liability management: in May 2026 American refinanced the 2014 term loans of about 1.1 billion due January 2027 and added 703 million of incremental term loans, maturing May 2033 at SOFR plus 3.00 percent; in the first quarter it re-established its three revolving facilities to March 2031 at about 3.1 billion in aggregate; the 2025 AAdvantage term loan was repriced to SOFR plus 2.75 percent. American prepaid the 8.50 percent senior secured notes of 1.0 billion, repaid a 629 million short-term term loan and prepaid 310 million of EETC equipment notes. Liquidity effect: total available liquidity rose to 11,763 at 2026-09-30 from 9,213 at 2025-12-31 (US$ millions, from the financial base), partly funded by the new borrowing. Credit effect: the maturity wall in 2027 eased (the 2014 term loans moved from 2027 to 2033), but the added EETC and equipment debt is secured on aircraft and adds to claims ahead of unsecured creditors; these EETC notes are direct obligations of American and in certain instances guaranteed by AAG (10-K page:189).

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: American is a highly leveraged airline whose credit rests on liquidity and asset-backed funding rather than on current earnings. The strongest support is liquidity of USD 11,763 million at 2026-09-30, with maturities extended during 2026 and recurring loyalty and card cash. The weakest point is earnings: operating income for the nine months of 2026 was USD 535 million against USD 1,042 million a year earlier, because unhedged fuel rose faster than revenue, leaving net debt at 6.04x last-twelve-month EBITDA and cash interest cover at 2.06x. The outcome will be decided by the fuel price and demand path, by access to financing for USD 24,056 million of aircraft and engine commitments, and by how the parent's support and intercompany claims behave. Confidence is medium.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Earnings have not kept up with fuel. For the nine months of 2026, American's revenue was USD 46,979 million against USD 40,628 million, while aircraft fuel and related taxes were USD 12,444 million against USD 8,017 million, and no fuel hedges were outstanding at 2026-09-30 [financial base: Earnings and cash flow quality; business context: Fuel hedging row, Documentary Fact]. Because fuel absorbed about seven tenths of the revenue gain, operating income fell to USD 535 million from USD 1,042 million. Fuel is the most volatile cost line and the exposure is open, so a further price rise lands directly on EBITDA, the denominator of every credit metric. This is a Documentary Fact for the figures and an Analyst Interpretation for the sensitivity.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Leverage is high and moved the wrong way on the ratio even as net debt fell. Net debt was USD 17,623 million at 2026-09-30, down from USD 19,443 million at 2025-12-31, yet net debt over EBITDA rose to 6.04x from 5.73x because last-twelve-month EBITDA fell to USD 2,916 million from USD 3,395 million; total debt of USD 25,876 million is 8.87x EBITDA [financial base: Leverage and coverage]. Cash interest cover is 2.06x, against 2.19x for FY2025 and 2.53x for FY2024. With cover near twice, small declines in EBITDA or increases in floating-rate interest have an outsized effect on debt service capacity. These ratios exclude operating leases (USD 6,592 million), pensions (USD 1,098 million) and fuel financing (USD 933 million), so the true burden is higher; EBITDA is derived by the analysis and not reported (Analyst Interpretation).

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Liquidity is the main support but is partly borrowed, and the maturity profile is lumpy. Liquidity was USD 11,763 million, made up of cash and short-term investments of USD 8,253 million and undrawn facilities of USD 3,510 million, up from USD 9,213 million at 2025-12-31, while USD 5,933 million of debt was issued in the nine months [financial base: Liquidity and covenants]. Principal due in 2028 is USD 7,861 million, the largest named year, with USD 631 million in the remainder of 2026 and USD 3,550 million in 2027. Liquidity comfortably covers the USD 4,181 million of principal due in the remainder of 2026 and 2027, but the 2028 concentration requires market access or cash accumulation; the 2014 term loan extension to 2033 shows that access exists at present. A cargo receivables facility of USD 50 million expires in December 2026, which is minor.

facts.text: Capital commitments and cash conversion limit free cash. Operating cash flow less capital expenditure was negative USD 132 million for the last twelve months, even though nine-month operating cash flow was USD 4,440 million, because the nine-month figure was lifted by seasonal growth in air traffic and loyalty liabilities [financial base: Earnings and cash flow quality]. Aircraft and engine purchase commitments total USD 24,056 million, with regional capacity commitments of USD 4,461 million and other purchase obligations of USD 19,612 million [financial base: Claims outside the debt figure]. The filing intends to fund deliveries with cash and long-term financing, so these commitments are a standing call on the market access that the liquidity position supports.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The parent relationship is a two-way credit link. AAG guarantees about USD 14.1 billion of American's debt, American guarantees AAG's USD 3,746 million of promissory notes, and American carries a net USD 10,430 million related-party receivable, mainly owed by AAG, which is not counted as liquidity [business context: Ownership, governance and behaviour, Documentary Fact rows]. American's 2025 borrowing was in part used to repay a parent convertible note. The mechanism is that value and support move between issuer and parent, so American's creditors are exposed to AAG's liquidity and to the performance of its intercompany balance, while the guarantee gives secured creditors a second obligor with no AAG collateral behind it. Governance behaviour is Mixed (Analyst Interpretation).

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. ### Source assessment
#### Combined-filing perimeter

The annual and quarterly reports are joint filings by the parent and the issuer, so every figure must be read with its perimeter. Evidence: the 10-K states the joint filing and its split. Mechanism: the same page of text carries parent and issuer numbers, so a careless read can attribute parent debt or earnings to the issuer. Consequence: downstream modules must take issuer figures from Item 8B of the 10-K and Item 1B of each 10-Q.

The issuer's own debt note is at 10-K page:217 and 10-Q Q3 page:30 to page:31; the issuer's financing narrative for 2026 is at 10-Q Q3 page:32 to page:36.
#### Authority and extraction fidelity

Filed statements control their facts; the decks are attributed management support. The text extraction is complete enough to locate every statement named above; that is extraction status, not a fidelity review of table cells against the original filing. Tables arrive as flattened text, so column alignment (for example AAG versus American columns in the liquidity table) must be confirmed by the consumer from the column headers.

#### Earnings presentations

The three decks are Exhibit 99.2 to the parent's results releases and are about AAG only. Evidence: the Q3 deck defines its net debt on a parent group basis. Mechanism: the reconciliation starts from group debt, leases and pensions and subtracts group cash, so it cannot be an issuer figure. Consequence: deck net debt, leverage targets and outlook are parent-level claims to be used as context and labelled so.

Current period Q3 2026 (quarter ended 2026-09-30, nine months 2026, and last twelve months to 2026-09-30, LTM); prior period FY2025 (year ended 2025-12-31), with FY2024 for comparison. Scope: the issuer's own reported statements, debt, liquidity, covenants, cash flow quality and the claims outside debt, taken from the issuer statements in Item 8B of the 10-K and Item 1B of each 10-Q.

Perimeter rule carried from the readiness handoff: American is a wholly-owned subsidiary of American Airlines Group Inc. (AAG) and files jointly with it. ## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Earnings have weakened sharply on fuel while gross debt is broadly stable: net debt over last-twelve-months EBITDA is 6.04x, cash interest cover is 2.06x, and liquidity is 11,763 in US$ millions, boosted by recent borrowing. | Medium | Covenant levels, executed debt terms and interim letters of credit are not supplied; EBITDA is derived, not reported. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Fuel expense rose faster than revenue, cutting operating income to 114 in the third quarter from 167 a year earlier. | Thin earnings leave little room to absorb a further fuel or demand shock. | High |

### Financial base view

The financial base for American is a highly levered airline whose reported earnings fell in 2026 while its balance sheet was kept intact by refinancing. On the issuer's own statements, operating income for the nine months of 2026 was 535 against 1,042 a year earlier, with fuel expense up by 4,427 over the same nine months, and the third quarter alone produced a pre-tax loss of 183. Last-twelve-month EBITDA, derived here as operating income plus depreciation and amortization, is 2,916, against 3,395 in FY2025 and 4,573 in FY2024. Gross debt including finance leases is 25,876 and net debt after unrestricted cash and short-term investments is 17,623, so net leverage is 6.04x and cash interest cover is 2.06x, both weaker than FY2025. Liquidity is large at 11,763 but was built partly through 5,933 of new debt, and the filings put 7,861 of principal due in 2028 plus a very large set of purchase commitments behind it. Parent-level facts matter for this issuer: American guarantees three parent promissory notes and carries a net 10,430 receivable from related parties, mainly the parent. Confidence in the base is medium, because the metrics are calculated by this analysis from filed statements and several covenant and document inputs are not supplied.

### Earnings and cash flow quality

Evidence: American's revenue for the nine months of 2026 was 46,979 against 40,628, an increase of 6,351, while fuel expense rose from 8,017 to 12,444, an increase of 4,427, and operating income fell from 1,042 to 535. In the third quarter revenue was 16,334 against 13,688, fuel 4,635 against 2,767, and operating income 114 against 167. Mechanism: fuel absorbed about seven tenths of the nine-month revenue gain (4,427 of 6,351, calculated below), and other cost lines (salaries, wages and benefits 14,019 against 13,058) rose as well, so incremental revenue converted to very little operating profit. The filing states that the company does not hedge fuel (Q3 10-Q page:45, "Our current policy is not to enter into transactions to hedge our fuel consumption"), so the exposure is open. Implication: coverage is thin, and a further fuel increase flows straight to EBITDA, which is the denominator of both leverage and interest cover.

Operating cash flow of 4,440 for the nine months against 2,229 looks strong but has a specific source: the filing attributes the increase mainly to working capital increases in air traffic liability and loyalty program liability and to changes in net receivables from related parties (Q3 10-Q page:63). Air traffic liability rose from 7,158 to 9,414 and the total loyalty program liability from 10,564 to 11,514 over the nine months, which are seasonal and advance-sale balances that reverse, not earnings. In FY2025 operating cash flow was 1,930 after a 1,701 outflow for net receivables from related parties, so cash generated by American was in part passed to affiliates. Operating cash flow less capital expenditure and aircraft purchase deposits was negative 1,786 in FY2025, positive 1,780 in the nine months of 2026, and negative 132 on the last twelve months (calculated below). Capital expenditure is sizeable at 2,660 in the nine months and is set to continue, given 24,056 of aircraft and engine purchase commitments (Q3 10-Q page:66).

Net income for the nine months was a loss of 231, including nonoperating special items of 259 of which 78 is an impairment of the equity investment in Republic Holdings (Q3 10-Q page:28). The special-items line within operating income is small (29 for the nine months), so EBITDA excluding it is within 3 percent of EBITDA as derived, as shown below.
### Leverage and coverage

Gross leverage is calculated on balance-sheet debt and finance leases, because that is the only debt aggregate the issuer statements print as a sum of components; net leverage deducts cash and short-term investments (not restricted cash). On this basis total debt over LTM EBITDA is 8.87x at 2026-09-30, against 7.44x at 2025-12-31 and 5.63x at 2024-12-31, and net debt over EBITDA is 6.04x, against 5.73x and 4.10x. Net debt itself fell from 19,443 to 17,623 over the nine months because cash and short-term investments rose from 5,816 to 8,253 while gross debt rose from 25,259 to 25,876; the ratio nevertheless rose because LTM EBITDA fell from 3,395 to 2,916. Mechanism: the cash build was funded by 5,933 of new borrowing in the nine months, so net leverage improves in dollars but not in ratio and the cash carries interest cost. Cash interest cover (EBITDA over interest paid, net) is 2.06x LTM, against 2.19x in FY2025 and 2.53x in FY2024. Interest paid is the issuer's net figure and the filing does not say whether it nets capitalised interest or interest income, which limits the measure.

The ratios exclude operating lease liabilities (6,592 at 2026-09-30), pension and postretirement obligations (1,098), fuel financing (933) and the parent guarantees described below. Management's own AAG net debt of 28,079 and its target of 3.0x net debt to EBITDAR are parent-level, lease and pension inclusive, and are not comparable to the issuer ratios here (Q3 deck page:6 and page:10). No attempt is made to restate American on the management definition, because the deck's pension figure (92) differs from the issuer balance sheet line (1,098) and the definitions cannot be reconciled from the supplied text.
### Debt structure and maturity profile

American's debt note (Q3 10-Q page:30 to page:31) lists, at 2026-09-30, secured debt of 25,575 in principal: the 2013 term loan (960, due February 2028), the 2014 term loan (1,850, now due May 2033), the 2023 term loan (1,078, due June 2029), 7.25% senior secured notes (750, due February 2028), 5.75% senior secured notes (2,750, amortising to April 2029), the 2021 and 2025 AAdvantage term loans (2,247 due April 2028 and 988 due May 2032), enhanced equipment trust certificates (EETCs, 9,332, 2027 to 2039, fixed rates 2.88% to 7.15%), equipment loans and other notes (4,926, 2027 to 2038) and special facility revenue bonds (694, 2031 to 2036). The 8.50% senior secured notes (1,000 at 2025-12-31), the 5.50% AAdvantage notes (583) and the unsecured short-term term loan (629) were repaid in the nine months. Count check: the table lists 12 secured lines (two of them, the 8.50% and 5.50% notes, now nil) and one unsecured line (the short-term term loan, now nil). Note total 25,575 less unamortised discount and costs of 344 gives 25,231, less current maturities of 3,580 gives long-term debt of 21,651 (calculated); the balance-sheet lines add finance leases of 109 current and 536 noncurrent (calculated), so debt including finance leases is 25,876.

Security and guarantors as printed in the 10-K: AAG guarantees the credit facilities (10-K page:222), the 7.25% and 8.50% secured notes (page:223 to page:224) and the AAdvantage financing, which is also guaranteed by special purpose subsidiaries and secured on AAdvantage program assets (page:226 to page:227). The EETC equipment notes are direct obligations of American and in certain instances guaranteed by AAG (10-K page:189). Guarantor detail for the 2026 EETCs and equipment loans is not stated in the Q3 10-Q. The co-issuer of the AAdvantage loans is AAdvantage Loyalty IP Ltd. (Q3 10-Q page:33).

Maturity profile (principal, from the contractual obligations table for American, calculated shares in the next section): remainder of 2026, 631; 2027, 3,550; 2028, 7,861; 2029, 3,884; 2030, 972; 2031 and thereafter, 8,677; total 25,575. The 2028 bucket is the largest of the named years. Instruments due in 2028 carry face balances of 960 (2013 term loan, February), 750 (7.25% notes, February) and 2,247 (2021 AAdvantage term loan, April), together 3,957 (calculated); the remainder of the 2028 amount is scheduled amortisation of other instruments. The filing prints only the aggregate by year, so the full split is not available. The May 2026 amendment moved the 2014 term loans from January 2027 to May 2033 and removed that 2027 maturity (Q3 10-Q page:32). Contractual finance lease obligations total 834 undiscounted, shown separately in the filing and not in the principal profile.
### Liquidity and covenants

Liquidity at 2026-09-30 is 11,763 (cash 1,094, short-term investments 7,159, undrawn facilities 3,510), against 9,213 at 2025-12-31, 10,787 at 2026-03-31 and 11,266 at 2026-06-30. By facility, availability is 363 (2013 revolver, matures March 2031), 1,296 (2014 revolver, March 2031), 1,451 (2023 revolver, March 2031) and 400 of other facilities, comprising a revolving credit facility of up to 350 extended to March 2028 and 50 under a cargo receivables facility that expires in December 2026 (Q3 10-Q page:31 and page:32 to page:33). The filing states there are no amounts drawn under the other facilities; it does not print letters of credit outstanding at 2026-09-30, and the 10-K shows none outstanding under the 2013 and 2014 revolvers at 2025-12-31 (page:220 to page:222). Availability is taken as printed, with the date gap noted. Restricted cash and short-term investments of 555 are excluded (Q3 10-Q page:26). Escrowed proceeds of about 633 held for holders of the 2026-2 EETCs are not American's assets and are not in cash or debt (Q3 10-Q page:35).

Covenants as printed (substantially the same wording in the 10-K and the Q3 10-Q): a significant portion of debt agreements require at least 2.0 billion of unrestricted cash and cash equivalents plus amounts available under revolving credit facilities; secured debt carries loan-to-value or collateral coverage tests, with consequences of additional collateral, cash withholding, prepayment or higher interest; the AAdvantage financing has a peak debt service coverage test that can trigger early repayment; the 7.25% notes pay 2.00% extra interest if the collateral coverage ratio is below 1.6 to 1.0 (10-K page:224). Management states compliance at the latest measurement dates. Headroom on the liquidity covenant cannot be measured exactly, because the covenant's definition of qualifying cash is not supplied. A conservative proxy using cash of 1,094 plus the three revolvers (3,110) gives 4,204, which is 2,204 above 2,000 (calculated below); it excludes short-term investments and the 400 of other facilities. The reported measured values of the collateral coverage and debt service coverage tests are Not supplied. The definition of these tests differs from the cash-based leverage and cover metrics computed here, which are not covenant measures.

### EBITDA

Q3 2026: 114 + 491 = 605; Q3 2025: 167 + 473 = 640. ### Ratios
### Liquidity
### Maturities and shares

Sum check: 631 + 3,550 + 7,861 + 3,884 + 972 + 8,677 = 25,575, equal to the principal total. Share of principal due in 2028: 7,861 / 25,575 = 30.7 percent. ### Earnings drivers

Nine-month revenue change: 46,979 - 40,628 = 6,351. Nine-month fuel change: 12,444 - 8,017 = 4,427. Fuel as a share of the revenue gain: 4,427 / 6,351 = 69.7 percent. Operating income change: 535 - 1,042 = -507. Q3 revenue change: 16,334 - 13,688 = 2,646; Q3 fuel change: 4,635 - 2,767 = 1,868. Gross proceeds of debt issued in the nine months: 5,933 (cash flow statement, Q3 10-Q page:27).
### Operating cash flow less capital expenditure

FY2024: 3,409 - 2,624 = 785. FY2025: 1,930 - 3,716 = -1,786. Nine months 2025: 2,229 - 2,103 = 126. Nine months 2026: 4,440 - 2,660 = 1,780. LTM: 4,141 - 4,273 = -132. ## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| American is the wholly-owned operating airline of a listed parent, with a hub network, a large loyalty business and open fuel exposure. Support runs both ways between issuer and parent. No sponsor or acquisition exists. | Medium | No debt documents, ratings or post-quarter filings are supplied, and group-level management claims are not issuer facts. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| American owns the airline and is wholly owned by the listed parent, with regional carriers sitting under the parent and paid by American. | Issuer credit depends on parent support, intercompany balances and regional capacity costs it does not control. | High |

| The loyalty program and co-branded card payments support revenue and secure part of the debt. | Loyalty cash is a durable inflow but is also pledged collateral, limiting what is free for other creditors. | Medium |
| Fuel is unhedged and rose sharply, with no hedges outstanding at the end of the third quarter. | Margin and cash flow stay exposed to fuel and demand shocks. | High |

| 2026 activity was refinancing and aircraft financing, not an acquisition or sponsor transaction. | Maturities were extended, but new secured debt adds to claims ahead of unsecured creditors. | Medium |
### Business and transaction view

American is the main operating airline of AAG, a listed holding company, and it is the issuer whose creditors this review serves. The business is a hub-based network carrier whose revenue is overwhelmingly passenger, with a loyalty program and co-branded card relationships that provide cash and collateral, and whose cost base is dominated by fuel, labor and regional capacity purchased from carriers under the parent. There is no financial sponsor, no pending acquisition and no dividend recapitalisation in the sources; the transaction record for the period is a sequence of refinancings, aircraft financings and facility amendments, plus a small set of aircraft purchase decisions in October 2026 after quarter end. The governance picture is Mixed rather than Supportive or Adverse: the parent guarantees a large share of American's debt and American guarantees parent notes and funds the parent through intercompany balances, both documented actions, while American has also repaid its own secured debt early. The main creditor consequences are structural (support running in both directions, secured debt ranking ahead of unsecured claims and collateral that includes the loyalty business) and operational (open fuel exposure and heavy fleet commitments). Confidence is medium because executed documents, ratings and any information after the Q3 10-Q are not supplied.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

No acquisition, sponsor transaction, dividend recapitalisation or change of control involving American is in the sources, and the context lists no deal terms, so that transaction fact is Insufficient Information for any such event and nothing is inferred. The financing record is executed and closed as reported in the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q (unaudited), covering the first nine months of 2026, and is American's own activity, with the parent a co-party to the credit agreements and a guarantor.

New debt in the period: American issued enhanced equipment trust certificates in several series. In March 2026 it borrowed 870 million of junior financing secured on aircraft already delivered (the 2026-1 Class (B)R financing, fixed rate 5.61 percent, maturing 2028 to 2029). In May 2026 it created the 2026-1 pass-through trusts (about 1.1 billion face, 32 aircraft). In June 2026 it issued 567 million of engine EETCs to refinance 228 million at maturity and raise 339 million of new borrowing. In August 2026 it created the 2026-2 trusts (about 1.3 billion face, 37 aircraft), of which about 692 million had been used to buy equipment notes at 2026-09-30 and about 633 million was held in escrow for holders, not reported as American's debt. It also borrowed 705 million of variable-rate equipment loans on aircraft. The use of proceeds is aircraft financing, and the filing states that proceeds of the nine months totalled about 4.1 billion for EETCs, equipment loans and other notes (page:46).

Refinancing and liability management: in May 2026 American refinanced the 2014 term loans of about 1.1 billion due January 2027 and added 703 million of incremental term loans, maturing May 2033 at SOFR plus 3.00 percent; in the first quarter it re-established its three revolving facilities to March 2031 at about 3.1 billion in aggregate; the 2025 AAdvantage term loan was repriced to SOFR plus 2.75 percent. American prepaid the 8.50 percent senior secured notes of 1.0 billion, repaid a 629 million short-term term loan and prepaid 310 million of EETC equipment notes. Liquidity effect: total available liquidity rose to 11,763 at 2026-09-30 from 9,213 at 2025-12-31 (US$ millions, from the financial base), partly funded by the new borrowing. Credit effect: the maturity wall in 2027 eased (the 2014 term loans moved from 2027 to 2033), but the added EETC and equipment debt is secured on aircraft and adds to claims ahead of unsecured creditors; these EETC notes are direct obligations of American and in certain instances guaranteed by AAG (10-K page:189).

Fundamental credit synthesis for AMERICAN AIRLINES, INC. (issuer id american-airlines-inc), as of 2026-11-05, pathway credit_snapshot, reporting currency USD. It combines the financial base and the business and transaction context for American as the issuer, with parent facts labelled.
## Sources
### Issuer sources
This synthesis reads no source text directly; its evidence is the upstream handoffs. The pinned issuer sources behind them are listed for traceability.
| Source file | sha256 |
| EX-99.2_2026-04-23_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl | 9a2e0cf77a5348cca76e4e1fa089b91044513dded2916dcf498cbc76a4f142fe |
| EX-99.2_2026-07-23_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl | 60d450333d317c8f5bcb2c0834ff53272fd96fa253d4a67d36813c30742d7ee9 |
| EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl | ce6723a4b2e59ac217d38de9b2fa855bbf5fa9fd11b713b0732222688fa7865b |
### Context
| Item | sha256 |
| context (user settings, not issuer evidence) | 4315193a9d24f5f5ddc6f4bf134c08d91788bf1e14ed0a34e81f98521fa4fc9b |
### Handoffs
| Module | sha256 | Role |
| CP-0 | d2c2217d545d90f74a5b8e3d65418442e5f1ebc0d6624ce35bbca3459b6fd9f3 | Source readiness and limits |
| CP-1 | ee800a14f4d54fb51366d1b36ecf9d88e3f7b9083ef36890e8e5611bb9bb03cd | Financial base: figures, leverage, liquidity, maturities, claims outside debt |
| CP-1A | b195565a04b618b13acdab6a311719fd1afa87d28a98e633f9b3fce9861b01df | Business, ownership, governance and transaction context |

Consistency with upstream: all figures are the financial base figures, unrecalculated. The business context handoff already corrects the locator for the aircraft and engine commitments (page 65 of the third-quarter 2026 report, not page 66). This synthesis adds no source facts beyond the handoffs.
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| American is highly leveraged and its earnings are thin, so its credit rests on liquidity and asset-backed funding. The outcome turns on fuel, access to financing for aircraft commitments, and parent support. | Medium | Debt documents, ratings and post-quarter information are not supplied, and EBITDA and ratios are derived, not reported. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Unhedged fuel rose faster than revenue, cutting nine-month operating income to USD 535 million from USD 1,042 million. | Earnings are thin and fuel-sensitive, which drives both leverage and interest cover. | High |
| Net debt over last-twelve-month EBITDA is 6.04x and cash interest cover is 2.06x. | Leverage is high and rose from the prior year-end; debt service has little earnings cushion. | Medium |

| Liquidity is USD 11,763 million, but part of it was borrowed in 2026 and USD 7,861 million of principal falls due in 2028. | Near-term liquidity is solid, with a concentrated refinancing in 2028 and large aircraft commitments behind it. | Medium |
| Support runs both ways with the parent, including USD 10,430 million owed to American by related parties. | Parent stress could reach American through guarantees and intercompany claims. | Medium |
### Credit view

American is a highly leveraged airline whose credit rests on liquidity and asset-backed funding rather than on current earnings. The strongest support is liquidity of USD 11,763 million at 2026-09-30, with maturities extended during 2026 and recurring loyalty and card cash. The weakest point is earnings: operating income for the nine months of 2026 was USD 535 million against USD 1,042 million a year earlier, because unhedged fuel rose faster than revenue, leaving net debt at 6.04x last-twelve-month EBITDA and cash interest cover at 2.06x. The outcome will be decided by the fuel price and demand path, by access to financing for USD 24,056 million of aircraft and engine commitments, and by how the parent's support and intercompany claims behave. Confidence is medium.
### Key findings

Earnings have not kept up with fuel. For the nine months of 2026, American's revenue was USD 46,979 million against USD 40,628 million, while aircraft fuel and related taxes were USD 12,444 million against USD 8,017 million, and no fuel hedges were outstanding at 2026-09-30 [financial base: Earnings and cash flow quality; business context: Fuel hedging row, Documentary Fact]. Because fuel absorbed about seven tenths of the revenue gain, operating income fell to USD 535 million from USD 1,042 million. Fuel is the most volatile cost line and the exposure is open, so a further price rise lands directly on EBITDA, the denominator of every credit metric. This is a Documentary Fact for the figures and an Analyst Interpretation for the sensitivity.

Leverage is high and moved the wrong way on the ratio even as net debt fell. Net debt was USD 17,623 million at 2026-09-30, down from USD 19,443 million at 2025-12-31, yet net debt over EBITDA rose to 6.04x from 5.73x because last-twelve-month EBITDA fell to USD 2,916 million from USD 3,395 million; total debt of USD 25,876 million is 8.87x EBITDA [financial base: Leverage and coverage]. Cash interest cover is 2.06x, against 2.19x for FY2025 and 2.53x for FY2024. With cover near twice, small declines in EBITDA or increases in floating-rate interest have an outsized effect on debt service capacity. These ratios exclude operating leases (USD 6,592 million), pensions (USD 1,098 million) and fuel financing (USD 933 million), so the true burden is higher; EBITDA is derived by the analysis and not reported (Analyst Interpretation).

Liquidity is the main support but is partly borrowed, and the maturity profile is lumpy. Liquidity was USD 11,763 million, made up of cash and short-term investments of USD 8,253 million and undrawn facilities of USD 3,510 million, up from USD 9,213 million at 2025-12-31, while USD 5,933 million of debt was issued in the nine months [financial base: Liquidity and covenants]. Principal due in 2028 is USD 7,861 million, the largest named year, with USD 631 million in the remainder of 2026 and USD 3,550 million in 2027. Liquidity comfortably covers the USD 4,181 million of principal due in the remainder of 2026 and 2027, but the 2028 concentration requires market access or cash accumulation; the 2014 term loan extension to 2033 shows that access exists at present. A cargo receivables facility of USD 50 million expires in December 2026, which is minor.

Capital commitments and cash conversion limit free cash. Operating cash flow less capital expenditure was negative USD 132 million for the last twelve months, even though nine-month operating cash flow was USD 4,440 million, because the nine-month figure was lifted by seasonal growth in air traffic and loyalty liabilities [financial base: Earnings and cash flow quality]. Aircraft and engine purchase commitments total USD 24,056 million, with regional capacity commitments of USD 4,461 million and other purchase obligations of USD 19,612 million [financial base: Claims outside the debt figure]. The filing intends to fund deliveries with cash and long-term financing, so these commitments are a standing call on the market access that the liquidity position supports.

The parent relationship is a two-way credit link. AAG guarantees about USD 14.1 billion of American's debt, American guarantees AAG's USD 3,746 million of promissory notes, and American carries a net USD 10,430 million related-party receivable, mainly owed by AAG, which is not counted as liquidity [business context: Ownership, governance and behaviour, Documentary Fact rows]. American's 2025 borrowing was in part used to repay a parent convertible note. The mechanism is that value and support move between issuer and parent, so American's creditors are exposed to AAG's liquidity and to the performance of its intercompany balance, while the guarantee gives secured creditors a second obligor with no AAG collateral behind it. Governance behaviour is Mixed (Analyst Interpretation).

Revenue durability is supported by the loyalty business. Co-branded card and other partner cash was USD 6.2 billion in 2025 at group level, with Citi the exclusive U.S. issuer from 2026 [business context: Loyalty and cards row, Documentary Fact]. This recurring cash supports debt service and also secures the AAdvantage financing, so it is both a strength for revenue visibility and a pledged asset that limits what is free for other creditors. The sources give no customer concentration beyond the card partners, which is an Insufficient Information item.

The capital structure is heavily secured. The debt is mostly secured on aircraft, engines, route and gate rights and the loyalty program, and secured instruments carry loan-to-value or collateral coverage tests that can force collateral, cash retention or prepayment [financial base: Debt structure and Liquidity and covenants]. Management states compliance, but covenant values and executed documents are not supplied, so headroom is not calculable beyond a conservative liquidity proxy of USD 4,204 million against a USD 2,000 million test. The mechanic is that unsecured and junior claims sit behind a large asset-backed claim base; the sources do not allow an assessment of collateral values or outcomes.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. Liquidity is large: USD 11,763 million at 2026-09-30, including USD 8,253 million of cash and short-term investments and USD 3,510 million of undrawn facilities, with revolver maturities extended to March 2031 (Documentary Fact; basis: financial base figures). Maturities were pushed out in 2026: the 2014 term loans moved from 2027 to 2033 and the 8.50 percent notes of USD 1.0 billion were prepaid, which reduced near-term refinancing pressure (Documentary Fact). Loyalty and co-branded card cash is recurring and contractual, which supports revenue visibility (Documentary Fact, with the management claim about premium revenue carried only as Management Language and not adopted). Net debt fell by USD 1,820 million to USD 17,623 million over the nine months to 2026-09-30 (Analyst Interpretation, calculated from the financial base net debt figures; the fall reflects cash built from borrowing). A network of nine hubs and a large alliance structure support demand (Documentary Fact).

Weaknesses. Earnings are thin: operating income for the nine months of 2026 was USD 535 million, and last-twelve-month EBITDA of USD 2,916 million supports leverage of 6.04x net and 8.87x gross (Documentary Fact for figures; Analyst Interpretation for the derived ratios). Interest cover is 2.06x on cash interest, leaving limited cushion (Analyst Interpretation). Fuel is fully unhedged and has risen sharply (Documentary Fact). The 2028 maturity of USD 7,861 million and the USD 24,056 million of aircraft commitments create concentrated future financing needs (Documentary Fact). The parent link adds guarantee exposure of USD 3,746 million and an intercompany receivable of USD 10,430 million outside liquidity (Documentary Fact). Operating cash flow less capital expenditure was negative USD 132 million over the last twelve months (Analyst Interpretation). The secured capital structure with collateral tests places unsecured claims behind an asset-backed claim base, and the executed documents that would define priority are not supplied (Insufficient Information).

Thesis (Analyst Interpretation): American's credit rests on a large, partly borrowed liquidity position and asset-backed access to financing that offset thin, fuel-sensitive earnings and high leverage, so the credit depends on fuel prices, demand and continued market access.
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Fuel and demand shock | No hedges; fuel was USD 12,444 million for nine months 2026 against USD 8,017 million; operating income USD 535 million | EBITDA and interest cover fall quickly; leverage rises | Critical |
| High leverage and weak cover | Net debt 6.04x and total debt 8.87x EBITDA; cover 2.06x | Little room to absorb a downturn; debt service sensitive to rates | Material |
| 2028 refinancing concentration | USD 7,861 million principal due 2028 | Needs market access or accumulated cash; liquidity is the buffer | Material |

| Fleet commitments | USD 24,056 million of aircraft and engine commitments against EBITDA of USD 2,916 million | Standing financing need; free cash flow negative on the last twelve months | Material |
| Parent linkage | Guarantees both ways and USD 10,430 million receivable | AAG stress reaches American; intercompany cash is not liquidity | Material |

| Secured structure and covenant tests | Loan-to-value and collateral tests; liquidity covenant of USD 2,000 million | Collateral calls or prepayment could drain liquidity under stress; headroom not measurable exactly | Material |
| Information limits | No debt documents, ratings or post-quarter data | Priority, headroom and recent events are untested | Minor |
## Calculations

None new. Every figure is a financial base figure, reproduced without arithmetic, apart from one difference stated in the strengths text: net debt of USD 19,443 million at 2025-12-31 less USD 17,623 million at 2026-09-30 is USD 1,820 million (19,443 - 17,623 = 1,820).
## Gaps
| Gap | Why it matters | Affects | Severity | Action |

| Executed debt documents, covenant levels and measured values are Not supplied | Priority, guarantor structure, collateral terms and headroom cannot be tested | Risks, assessment confidence | Material | Obtain indentures, credit agreements and compliance certificates |
| Credit ratings are Not supplied | No external view and rating-linked pricing cannot be tested | Assessment | Minor | None in the pack |

| EBITDA and the ratios are derived, not reported; interest paid may net capitalised interest | Leverage and cover depend on the stated definition | Key findings | Minor | Keep definitions with every ratio |

| Interim letters of credit under facilities and discrete-quarter cash flows are Not supplied | Undrawn facility availability may be overstated; Q3 cash conversion is not shown | Liquidity view | Minor | Use printed availability and flag |

| The business context handoff recorded no readiness judgment for this module, which is a signal that limits confidence to below High | Confidence is held at Medium | Assessment | Minor | None; stated here |
| Nothing is supplied after the third-quarter report of 2026-10-22 | Developments to the cutoff are untested | All findings | Minor | None in the pack |

| Customer concentration beyond card partners and restricted-payment terms for distributions to the parent are Not supplied | Revenue concentration and leakage capacity cannot be assessed | Strengths and weaknesses | Minor | Obtain documents |
## Next module

Pass to CP-5 the conclusions above with their basis: each finding cites the financial base and business context sections named in brackets, categories are tagged, and the open gaps are listed. CP-5 should trace each figure to its handoff and check that the key findings, risks and strengths text agree with the upstream registers, in particular the leverage, liquidity, maturity and parent-linkage figures.
